title: Tzedakah, Guests and Saving a Life
bigQuestion: What do the rabbis of the Talmud say a person owes to the poor, the guest, the sick and the person in danger?

story.title: The Radio on Shabbat
story.kicker: It is Saturday morning, a day of rest, and a radio crackles: someone needs help right now.
paragraphs: Saturday morning in a Chicago neighborhood. No cars in the driveway. Uncle Ari's family walks to synagogue on *Shabbat*, the Jewish day of rest. They do not drive. They do not turn on lights. Eight-year-old Noa likes the quiet. Then a small radio on Uncle Ari's belt crackles. A voice says an address. Someone has fallen and cannot breathe well.

Uncle Ari runs. He jumps into a white ambulance parked on the street and drives off. Noa stares. "Isn't it Shabbat?" she asks her mother. "You told me we never drive on Shabbat." Her mother nods. "We don't. Unless a life is in danger. Then the rule changes."

Later, Uncle Ari comes home. The person is at the hospital and will be fine. Noa still has her question. Uncle Ari pulls a book off the shelf. It is a tractate of the Talmud called Yoma. "Long ago," he says, "the rabbis asked your question. What if a wall falls on someone on Shabbat? Do you dig, or do you wait for sunset?"

"You dig," Noa says. "Right," says Uncle Ari. "The rabbis said you dig. Even if you are not sure anyone is under there. Even if it might be too late. They had a name for it: *pikuach nefesh*, saving a life. A rabbi named Shmuel said the Torah's rules are for living by, not for dying by." Noa thinks about the quiet morning and the loud radio. Both, she decides, are part of the same day.
story.think: Why do you think the rabbis said to dig even when you are not sure someone is trapped?

lessons.title: Tzedakah Means Justice
lessons.mainIdea: In Jewish tradition, giving to the poor is called tzedakah, from the word for justice, because the poor have a right to it.
reading: In English, giving to the poor is called charity. The word comes from a Latin word for love. The Hebrew word is different. *Tzedakah* comes from *tzedek*, which means justice. In Jewish tradition, giving to the poor is not only a kind feeling. It is something the poor are owed. It is a matter of fairness.

The Torah sets this up. In Leviticus, a farmer must leave the corners of the field for the poor. That is called *pe'ah*, the corner. Dropped grain stays on the ground for them too. In Deuteronomy, a person must 'open your hand' to a poor neighbor. The Mishnah has a whole tractate called Pe'ah about these rules.

The Mishnah's first lines in Pe'ah are famous. They list things that have no set limit. One is the corner of the field. Another is acts of kindness. Another is study of Torah. Jewish readers have taken this to mean that giving has no top. There is a least amount, the rabbis said, but no most.

words.d: giving to the poor; the word comes from tzedek, justice
the corner of a field left unharvested for the poor; also a tractate of the Mishnah
justice; fairness

look.title: Open Your Hand
look.text: The Torah says that if there is a poor person among you, you must not harden your heart or shut your hand against him. You must open your hand and lend him enough for whatever he needs.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 15:7–8, paraphrased from the JPS Tanakh, 1917
look.prompt: The verse uses the words 'heart' and 'hand.' What is the difference between hardening a heart and shutting a hand?

check.q: What Hebrew word is tzedakah built from?
check.why: Tzedakah comes from tzedek, justice. The idea is that the poor are owed help, not just given it.

check.q: What is pe'ah?
choices: The corner of a field left for the poor
check.why: Pe'ah is the corner of the field the Torah tells farmers to leave for the poor; Mishnah Pe'ah is named for it.

check.q: What does the first Mishnah of Pe'ah say about acts of kindness?
choices: They must be done once a year
check.why: Mishnah Pe'ah 1:1 lists acts of kindness among the things that have no fixed measure.

lessons.title: Everyone Gives
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says even a poor person who lives on tzedakah gives tzedakah, and it sets a floor and a ceiling for giving.
reading: Who has to give? The Gemara in tractate Gittin gives a surprising answer. Even a poor person who is fed by tzedakah must give tzedakah. Why? Because giving is part of being a person, not a thing only rich people do. A small gift from a poor person counts fully. This is a well-known teaching in Jewish life today.

How much? Jewish custom, based on the Torah's tithe, is about a tenth of what you earn. The rabbis also set a top. At a meeting in a town called Usha, about 1,900 years ago, they ruled that a person should not give away more than a fifth. The reason is kind: a person who gives too much may become poor too.

Rabbinic tradition also cares how you give. The Gemara says the poor person's face matters. If someone gives with a sour look, the gift loses its worth. A kind word with the gift counts as much as the gift. Some Jewish readers today say this is the heart of tzedakah: the dignity of the one who receives.

words.d: a tractate of the Talmud; one page in it teaches that even the poor give tzedakah
a tenth part, set aside as a gift
a town in the Galilee where rabbis met and made rulings after the year 135 CE

look.title: How Much to Give
rows: Coins given out of 100, at a tenth
Coins given out of 100, at a fifth (the most, ruled at Usha)
Coins kept out of 100, after giving a fifth
look.cite: Ketubot 50a on the ruling at Usha; the custom of a tenth from the Torah's tithe
look.prompt: Why might the rabbis set a top amount for giving, not only a least amount?

check.q: According to the Gemara in Gittin, who must give tzedakah?
choices: Even a poor person who lives on tzedakah
check.why: Gittin 7b says even a poor person supported by tzedakah must give some tzedakah.

check.q: What top amount did the rabbis at Usha set for giving?
check.why: Ketubot 50a records the ruling at Usha: do not give away more than a fifth, so you do not become poor yourself.

check.q: What does the Gemara say about giving with a sour face?
check.why: The rabbis taught that how you give matters; a sour look takes away from the gift.

lessons.title: The Secret Gift
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis prized giving in secret, so the poor are not shamed, and Maimonides put it near the top of his ladder of giving.
reading: The Mishnah describes a room in the Temple in Jerusalem. It was called the chamber of secrets. People who wanted to give slipped money in with no one watching. Poor people from good families took money out the same way. No one saw who gave. No one saw who took. Nobody had to feel shame.

The Gemara tells a story about a rabbi named Mar Ukva. Every day he dropped coins by a poor man's door and hurried away. One day the poor man decided to see who it was. He waited by the door. Mar Ukva and his wife saw him coming and ran. They hid in a hot oven so the man would not see them. Mar Ukva chose burnt feet over shaming a neighbor.

About 800 years ago, a Jewish scholar named *Maimonides* wrote a ladder of giving. It has eight steps. Near the top is giving where neither person knows the other. At the very top is helping a person so they no longer need help at all: a loan, a job, a business partner. Jewish groups still teach this ladder.

words.d: a room in the Temple where gifts were left and taken with no one watching
a Babylonian rabbi in the Gemara who gave to the poor in secret
a Jewish scholar and doctor, c. 1138–1204, who wrote a ladder of eight kinds of giving

look.title: The Ladder of Giving
look.text: Maimonides lists eight levels of giving. The highest is to help a poor person stand on their own, with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so that they need no more help. Next is giving where the giver does not know who receives and the receiver does not know who gave.
look.cite: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–8, paraphrased
look.prompt: Why might helping someone find work rank above handing them money?

check.q: What was the chamber of secrets?
choices: A room where gifts were left and taken unseen
check.why: Mishnah Shekalim 5:6 describes the chamber of secrets, where giving and taking were done without being seen.

check.q: Why did Mar Ukva hide in an oven?
choices: So the poor man would not know who gave
check.why: Ketubot 67b: Mar Ukva ran into an oven rather than let the poor man learn who had been giving to him.

check.q: What is the top step of Maimonides' ladder?
choices: Helping a person so they no longer need help
check.why: Maimonides puts helping someone become self-supporting, through work or a loan, at the top.

lessons.title: Guests Before Everything
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says welcoming guests is even greater than greeting the Divine Presence, and it learns this from Abraham.
reading: In Genesis, Abraham is sitting at his tent door on a hot day. Three strangers appear. He runs to them. He bows. He brings water for their feet. He asks Sarah to bake. He serves the meal himself and stands while they eat. Readers of the Torah have long seen Abraham as the model of *hospitality*, welcoming guests.

The Gemara in tractate Shabbat makes a bold claim from this story. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the *Shekhinah*, the Divine Presence. How does he know? In the story, Abraham seems to be speaking with God when the strangers appear. Yet he turns to greet them first.

This teaching is written on the walls of many Jewish homes and schools. In Pirkei Avot, a sage says, 'Let your house be open wide, and let the poor be members of your household.' Jewish families of many kinds, Orthodox, Conservative and Reform, invite guests to Shabbat meals. Many say this page of Talmud is why.

words.d: welcoming guests warmly; in Hebrew, hakhnasat orchim
a rabbinic name for God's presence in the world
'Chapters of the Fathers,' a tractate of short sayings by the rabbis

look.title: Abraham's Guests, by the Numbers
rows: Strangers who came to Abraham's tent (Genesis 18:2)
Measures of fine flour Sarah baked (Genesis 18:6)
Abraham's age just before, at his circumcision (Genesis 17:24)
look.prompt: The Gemara says Abraham was resting after his circumcision. How does his age make his running to the guests more striking?

check.q: Who is the Talmud's model of welcoming guests?
check.why: Shabbat 127a learns hospitality from Abraham running to greet three strangers in Genesis 18.

check.q: What does Rav say welcoming guests is greater than?
check.why: Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Shekhinah, the Divine Presence.

check.q: Which tractate holds the saying 'Let your house be open wide'?
check.why: Pirkei Avot 1:5 records the saying about an open house and the poor as members of the household.

lessons.title: Visiting the Sick
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis treated visiting the sick as a duty, and they told stories to show how much a visit can do.
reading: The Gemara in tractate Nedarim tells a story about Rabbi Akiva. One of his students got sick. No one went to see him. Rabbi Akiva went himself. He swept the floor and tidied the room. The student said, 'Rabbi, you have brought me back to life.' Rabbi Akiva then taught: whoever does not visit the sick, it is as if he sheds blood.

The same page has a saying from Rabbi Acha bar Chanina. Each person who visits takes away one-sixtieth of the illness. Others asked: then sixty visitors would cure anyone? The Gemara answers: only if each one cares as much as the sick person cares. The point is not magic. The point is that visits help.

Why is this a duty? The Gemara in Sotah gives a reason. It says God visited Abraham when he was healing. So people should visit the sick too. Jewish tradition calls this *bikkur cholim*, visiting the sick. Many synagogues in Chicago and everywhere have a bikkur cholim group that visits hospitals.

words.d: visiting the sick; a duty in Jewish tradition
a great teacher in the Land of Israel, c. 50–135 CE
a tractate of the Talmud; its pages 39b–40a discuss visiting the sick

look.title: Rabbi Akiva Sweeps the Floor
look.text: A student of Rabbi Akiva fell ill, and the sages did not visit him. Rabbi Akiva went in to visit him. Because he swept and sprinkled the floor before him, the student lived. He said, 'My teacher, you have given me life.' Rabbi Akiva went out and taught: anyone who does not visit the sick, it is as if he sheds blood.
look.cite: Nedarim 40a, paraphrased; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: What did Rabbi Akiva actually do in the room? Why might such a small thing matter so much?

check.q: What did Rabbi Akiva do when he visited his sick student?
choices: He swept and tidied the room
check.why: Nedarim 40a says Rabbi Akiva swept and sprinkled the floor, and the student said it gave him life.

check.q: What does bikkur cholim mean?
check.why: Bikkur cholim is the Hebrew name for visiting the sick.

check.q: How much of the illness does one visitor take away, says Rabbi Acha bar Chanina?
check.why: Nedarim 39b: one-sixtieth. The Gemara adds that this works only for a visitor who truly cares.

lessons.title: Kindness Bigger Than Money
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud says acts of kindness reach further than money, and it extends care to the poor and sick of every people.
reading: The Gemara in Sukkah compares two things. One is tzedakah, giving money. The other is *gemilut chasadim*, acts of kindness. Rabbi Elazar says kindness is greater in three ways. Money helps only the poor; kindness helps rich and poor. Money uses only your hand; kindness uses your whole self. Money helps only the living; kindness can honor the dead.

The Talmud also asks who is owed this care. In tractate Gittin, the rabbis rule that Jews support the poor of other peoples along with the poor of the Jewish people. They visit the sick of other peoples. They bury the dead of other peoples. The reason given is *darkhei shalom*, the ways of peace.

Readers today differ on how far these words reach. Some see them as a practical rule for living side by side. Others see them as a full call to care for every person. The course does not settle that. But notice the move: a rule made for one group is opened to the stranger. The two threads of this course, argument and mercy, meet here.

words.d: acts of kindness done with your own body and time, not only money
'the ways of peace,' a reason the rabbis give for caring for people of other groups

look.title: Three Ways Kindness Is Bigger
look.text: Rabbi Elazar in Sukkah 49b: tzedakah is done with money, kindness with money or with your body; tzedakah goes to the poor, kindness to poor and rich; tzedakah goes to the living, kindness to the living and the dead. Think of one act of kindness that fits each of the three.
look.prompt: Name one act of kindness that uses your body, one for someone who is not poor, and one that honors someone who has died.

check.q: Who does Rabbi Elazar say tzedakah helps, compared with kindness?
choices: Tzedakah helps only the poor; kindness helps rich and poor
Tzedakah helps everyone; kindness helps only the rich
check.why: Sukkah 49b: money reaches only the poor, but acts of kindness reach rich and poor alike.

check.q: What reason does Gittin give for supporting the poor of other peoples?
choices: Darkhei shalom, the ways of peace
check.why: Gittin 61a says these acts are done 'for the ways of peace,' darkhei shalom.

check.q: What does gemilut chasadim mean?
check.why: Gemilut chasadim are acts of kindness done with one's own effort, like visiting or comforting.

lessons.title: Move the Stones
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah in Yoma says that when a life may be in danger, you break Shabbat to save it, even if you are not sure.
reading: *Shabbat* is the Jewish day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Jewish tradition holds that the Torah forbids work on that day. The Mishnah lists 39 kinds of work. Digging, carrying and lighting a fire are on the list. So what happens if a wall falls on someone on Shabbat?

The Mishnah in tractate Yoma answers. If rubble falls on a person, you clear it away. Even if you are not sure anyone is under it. Even if you are not sure the person is alive. You keep digging until you know. The rabbis called this *pikuach nefesh*, saving a life. It sets aside almost every other rule.

The Gemara asks: how do we know? Several rabbis give proofs. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says, break one Shabbat for him, so he can keep many Shabbatot. Shmuel gives a verse from Leviticus: the rules are given so that a person 'shall live by them.' He adds: and not die by them. The Gemara says Shmuel's proof is the strongest.

words.d: the Jewish day of rest, from Friday sunset to Saturday night
saving a life; in Jewish law, it sets aside almost every other rule
the tractate about the Day of Atonement; its eighth chapter discusses saving a life

look.title: Live by Them
look.text: Ye shall therefore keep My statutes, and Mine ordinances, which if a man do, he shall live by them: I am the LORD.
look.prompt: Shmuel read 'live by them' as 'and not die by them.' Is that what the words say, or is it a reading he adds? Explain.

check.q: What does the Mishnah in Yoma say to do if rubble falls on someone on Shabbat?
choices: Clear it away, even if you are not sure anyone is there
Only call out to the person
check.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:7: you clear the rubble, even in doubt, because a life may be at stake.

check.q: Which verse does Shmuel use to prove that saving a life comes first?
choices: Proverbs 2:20, the way of good men
check.why: Yoma 85b: Shmuel reads Leviticus 18:5, 'live by them,' as 'and not die by them.'

check.q: What does pikuach nefesh mean?
check.why: Pikuach nefesh means saving a life. Jewish law places it above almost every other rule.

lessons.title: One Life, a Whole World
lessons.mainIdea: A famous Mishnah in Sanhedrin says that whoever saves a single life is counted as if they saved a whole world.
reading: The Mishnah in tractate *Sanhedrin* describes a courtroom. A person is on trial for their life. Before the witnesses speak, the judges warn them. A mistake here cannot be undone. Then the judges explain why one life matters so much. The first human, they say, was created alone.

From that, the Mishnah draws a lesson. Whoever destroys a single life is counted as if they destroyed a whole world. Whoever saves a single life is counted as if they saved a whole world. The Mishnah adds another reason. Since all people come from one person, no one can say, 'My father was greater than yours.'

This line is quoted all over the world today. It is carved on memorials. It appears in films. Scholars note that old handwritten copies say 'a single life.' Some later printed copies say 'a single life of Israel.' Most historians think the shorter words are older. Either way, Jewish readers have used this Mishnah to teach that every person is a world.

words.d: the high court in ancient Jewish tradition; also the tractate about courts and judges
a person who tells a court what they saw
a book copied by hand, before printing

look.title: As If a Whole World
look.text: The Mishnah says the first human was created alone to teach that whoever destroys a single life is counted as if he destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single life is counted as if he saved a whole world.
look.cite: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, paraphrased; compare Michael L. Rodkinson, Babylonian Talmud, 1896–1903
look.prompt: The Mishnah says this to witnesses in a court. Why would judges want witnesses to hear it before they speak?

check.q: In Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, who is being spoken to?
check.why: The Mishnah gives the warning judges say to witnesses before a trial where a life is at stake.

check.q: Why does the Mishnah say the first human was created alone?
choices: To teach that one life is like a whole world
check.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 says one person was created to teach that a single life equals a whole world.

check.q: What do scholars say about the words 'a single life' in old handwritten copies?
check.why: Most historians think the shorter reading, 'a single life,' is older than copies that add 'of Israel.'

lessons.title: Rules for Mercy
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis made mercy into clear rules, with a few firm limits, and Jewish communities today live by them.
reading: The Mishnah in Yoma gives more cases. On Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, Jewish tradition holds that adults fast all day. But a sick person who needs food is fed. A pregnant woman who smells food and feels faint is fed. The Mishnah says to listen to doctors. If the sick person says they need food, they are fed even if the doctors disagree.

Are there limits? The Gemara says yes, a very short list. In Sanhedrin, the rabbis say a person may not kill another to save their own life. The Gemara asks a sharp question: who says your blood is redder than his? Later rabbis count only three rules that may never be broken, even to live. Every other rule gives way to life.

Today, Jewish doctors, nurses and volunteer ambulance drivers in many cities answer calls on Shabbat. Orthodox, Conservative and Reform rabbis all teach that this is right. They point to Yoma 85. Rabbinic tradition turned a feeling, mercy, into a rule you can follow at 8 a.m. on a Saturday. That is what this unit has been about.

words.d: the Day of Atonement, a fast day in the Jewish year
to go without food and drink for a set time

look.title: A Feeling Becomes a Rule
look.text: Case one: a girl with a fever on Yom Kippur says she is too weak to fast. Case two: a man's radio calls him to an ambulance on Shabbat. Case three: a boy finds a stranger's wallet with a name inside. For each case, name the rule from this unit that applies and the tractate it comes from.
look.prompt: Which of the three cases is about pikuach nefesh, which is about returning a lost object, and which one could be both?

check.q: What does the Mishnah in Yoma say about a sick person on Yom Kippur?
choices: They are fed if they need food
check.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:5 says a sick person is fed on the advice of experts, and even on their own word if they insist.

check.q: What question does the Gemara ask about killing to save yourself?
choices: Who says your blood is redder?
check.why: Sanhedrin 74a: 'Who says your blood is redder than his?' You may not take a life to save your own.

check.q: Which page do rabbis of many kinds point to for driving an ambulance on Shabbat?
check.why: Yoma 85a–b is the main discussion of pikuach nefesh, saving a life on Shabbat.

review.q: Tzedakah comes from the word for what?
review.why: Tzedakah comes from tzedek, justice. Giving to the poor is treated as something owed.

review.q: Who must give tzedakah, according to Gittin 7b?
choices: Even the poor who receive it
review.why: The Gemara says even a poor person who is supported by tzedakah gives tzedakah.

review.q: What did the chamber of secrets in the Temple make possible?
review.why: Mishnah Shekalim 5:6: gifts went in and out unseen, so no one had to feel shame.

review.q: What is at the top of Maimonides' ladder of giving?
review.why: Maimonides ranks helping someone become self-supporting, through a job or loan, as the highest form.

review.q: From whose story does the Talmud learn that guests come first?
review.why: Shabbat 127a learns hospitality from Abraham running to greet three strangers in Genesis 18.

review.q: What did Rabbi Akiva teach after visiting his sick student?
choices: Whoever does not visit the sick is as if he sheds blood
Sweeping is a kind of work
review.why: Nedarim 40a: Rabbi Akiva taught that not visiting the sick is like shedding blood.

review.q: What does 'darkhei shalom' mean in Gittin 61a?
review.why: Darkhei shalom, the ways of peace, is the reason given for caring for the poor and sick of other peoples.

review.q: Which teaching says a person should break one Shabbat so they can keep many?
review.why: Yoma 85b records Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's reason for saving a life on Shabbat.
